title: Before the sun goes down (Ephesians 4:25–32)
hook: be angry but don't sin; be kind, tender-hearted, forgiving
tomorrow: why would a man in chains write about armor?

segments.voice: Yesterday: one body, one Lord, one faith, a unity kept by a long fuse. Today, what Paul says for the moment the fuse runs out.
screen: `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH.` → `WHEN THE FUSE RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: The fight happened at four. It's nine now, and you're still replaying it in the shower, winning this time. Paul has a line for exactly this, and it surprises people: "Be ye angry, and sin not." Not a ban on anger. He seems to expect it. What he cares about is how long it stays, and he sets the deadline in the very next words: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Sunset. Anger can come in the door. It isn't allowed to move in and unpack.
screen: `STILL REPLAYING IT AT NINE.` → `BE YE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.` → `THE DEADLINE: SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Here's one to tell a friend: be ye angry, and sin not wasn't new with Paul. His words echo a line from Psalm four, as it reads in the old Greek translation of the Psalms. Why the deadline? "Neither give place to the devil." Give place: hand over a room. Anger kept overnight, then a week, then years, becomes a room something else can live in. Then Paul gives a run of commands, and each has the same shape: stop one thing, start its opposite. Lying gives way to truth, "for we are members one of another." Stealing gives way to giving: "let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth." Harsh talk gives way to words that "minister grace unto the hearers." Then the list to clear out: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you." And what moves into the empty room? "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you." Paul doesn't say forgive because they've earned it. He says forgive as you've been forgiven. One honest note: settling anger isn't the same as rushing back to someone who hurts you. Sometimes the step before sunset happens inside you.
screen: `AN ECHO OF PSALM FOUR.` · `DON'T GIVE IT A ROOM.` · `STOP ONE THING, START ITS OPPOSITE.` · `FORGIVE AS YOU'VE BEEN FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `KIND, TENDERHEARTED.`

segments.voice: Name one anger you're carrying today, in a single sentence. Name what keeps you holding it: pride, fear, or just being right. Then choose one step before sunset, a short apology, a kind word, or, where talking isn't safe, a quiet decision to stop replaying it.
Before the sun goes down. Paul's deadline on anger: feel it, don't sin in it, and don't let it stay the night.
screen: `BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: kind, tenderhearted, forgiving, as you've been forgiven. The sun's still up. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christian couples and families take Ephesians 4:26 as a rule not to let a quarrel run overnight, and Ephesians 4:32 is read in some churches at weddings and services of reconciliation.

match.prompt: stop one thing, start another — tap the pairs.
pairs: even as God… hath forgiven you

myth: the Bible says all anger is a sin
a popular belief. be ye angry, and sin not: Paul expects anger and limits how long it stays.
Paul says forgive people because they deserve it
even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you: forgiven people forgive.
Paul's cure for stealing is working so you can give
that he may have to give to him that needeth.

fork.setup: a coworker admits he's been taking supplies home from the office and wants to stop for good. what's Paul's replacement?
options: work with his hands at something good, so he has something to give.
just stop; nothing needs to take the habit's place.
confess in front of everyone and pay a fine.
fork.reveal: let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour… that he may have to give to him that needeth. every command in the passage swaps a harm for its opposite.

original.note: Greek: anger, wrath. One of the words in Paul's list to put away, Ephesians 4:31.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't let the sun go down on your anger is just marriage advice.
what it means: Paul allows anger but sets a deadline, then swaps each harm for its opposite: lying for truth, stealing for giving, bitterness for kindness.
what a scholar hears: be ye angry, and sin not echoes Psalm 4:4 in the old Greek translation (the King James Psalm reads stand in awe, and sin not).
guess: settling anger the same day it starts
a curfew for children before dark
an evening prayer said at sunset

chat.says: snapped at dad about oven times in front of everyone. he went quiet. sun sets at like 6.
options: Then go before 6. Own your part, kindly. Paul doesn't ban anger; he sets a clock on it.
Give it a week. He's the parent; he should come to you first if he's upset.
Act normal. Paul says real Christians never feel angry, so just move past it.
chat.meaning: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Then: kind, tenderhearted, forgiving, as you've been forgiven.
